Tu peux tout à fait dire « très + adjectif » : c'est parfaitement correct.

Mais le français est une langue riche. Tu peux aussi utiliser des mots plus précis pour apporter de la nuance et enrichir ton vocabulaire.

Ancien : qui existe depuis longtemps ou qui date d'une époque passée. Selon le contexte, il peut parfois remplacer très vieux.
Exemple : C'est un bâtiment ancien.

Crasseux : très sale, couvert de saleté.
Exemple : Ses vêtements étaient crasseux.

Impeccable : parfaitement propre ou sans défaut.
Exemple : La cuisine est impeccable.

Muet : qui ne parle pas ou qui ne fait aucun bruit. Selon le contexte, il peut parfois remplacer très silencieux.
Exemple : La salle est restée muette.

Assourdissant : tellement fort qu'il est difficile à supporter.
Exemple : Le bruit des moteurs était assourdissant.

Hilarant : extrêmement drôle, qui fait beaucoup rire.
Exemple : Ce film est hilarant.

Exécrable : extrêmement mauvais, de très mauvaise qualité.
Exemple : Le service était exécrable.

Avais-tu trouvé ce dernier mot ? Ou en connais-tu un autre ? Écris ta réponse en commentaire !

🇯🇵 Feminine vs Masculine Japanese

Did you know that men and women often use different words and expressions in casual Japanese?
In this video, you'll learn everyday phrases that sound more feminine or more masculine while expressing the same meaning.

🔹 Feminine：すごい（sugoi） Masculine：すげえ（sugee） → Awesome
すげえ is a rough, masculine slang version of すごい that's commonly heard among men, especially in anime and casual conversations.

🔹 Feminine：本当？（hontō?） Masculine：マジか？（maji ka?） → Really?
マジか？ is a very casual, masculine reaction used when you're surprised or can't believe something.

🔹 Feminine：がんばって（ganbatte） Masculine：がんばれ（ganbare） → Do your best
Both encourage someone, but がんばれ sounds stronger, more direct, and more masculine.

🔹 Feminine：やめて（yamete） Masculine：やめろ（yamero） → Stop it
やめろ is a forceful command often heard in action movies, anime, and heated situations.

🔹 Feminine：早く（hayaku） Masculine：はよしろ（hayo shiro） → Hurry up
はよしろ is a rough, masculine way to tell someone to hurry up. It's very casual and should only be used with people you're close to or in informal situations.

💡 These are general tendencies in casual Japanese. Individual speech varies, and many expressions can be used by anyone depending on the situation, personality, and relationship.

Give me a 🙋🏻‍♀️ if you’re a learner who freezes when it comes to actually speaking!

It’s the biggest barrier for many many people.

We don’t want to speak until we can do it perfectly. We don’t want to be judged while we fumble etc.

But you know what??

Fumbling = progress. Mistakes = necessary.

You can’t learn to ride a bike from reading about it.

You also can’t learn to speak without speaking. You can learn great tips & tricks, you can learn vocabulary- but you NEEED to put it into practice to speak it.

I wish I’d started using my French ASAP! I would have found fluency much more quickly.

This is why I teach my students to speak as soon as we learn words together. We learn a word? We say it. We use it. I encourage them to put it into practice in real life contexts immediately.

I work to ensure they don’t have that mental barrier like I did. ♥️

I am no Spanish teacher but I am surely a Latina inside. I do not speak any other language to my son since he was born (sometimes the occasional Hebrew and Brazilian Portuguese come out).

Now this Spanish language extends to my son's playgroup, who are Filipino-Americans. I do not teach them. I simply speak it without imposing it to them.

Most of the time, I sing. Kids love adults who sing, especially if it's their primary caregiver. I was already 25 years old when I learned Spanish and I also leaned into songs for learning. I did not go to a Spanish language lesson because I know I am someone who doesn't learn in a classroom setting. I prefer the in-person action and application!

Some people warn me that it might be a bit too much that I speak to my son in several languages at an early age (plus my husband's Swiss German). They said it might be confusing.

But what most people don't know is that, scientifically, in the first 5 years of life, children's brains are incredibly flexible. This means they can form neural connections quickly making language acquisition easier compared to adults.

Kids also have the extraordinary ability to notice and absorb patterns in speech. They don't consciously study grammar rules but they naturally pick up tones and sounds by listening.

It's fascinating, isn't it? Often, our society treats kids under age 5 as helpless beings and we don't teach them things. We just give them 10,000 toys that they don't even want to play with.

When in fact, this age window is when we should be bombarding them with new learnings and experiences (such as language).

However, the challenge in this age is that the child won't necessarily learn to speak another language if the primary caregiver is not speaking it

dumb things I did to become a better Director

1. Studying the classics. I’m talking 1940s and 50s cinema. Modern films are great but the golden era had a way of storytelling that most current people ignore. So, make sure u go back in time and watch em.

2. Saying "yes" before I was ready. When a client asked for a specific style I’d never touched, I agreed instantly. I didn't have the skill yet, but I had the confidence to figure it out by the deadline.

3. Investing in a vision. If a concept was big enough, I’d invest in the production myself. Don't do this on everything, only if essential!

4. Treating movies like homework. I sit down with a notebook and breakdown every scene. If a shot works I write down why it works.

5. Being the "annoying" guy on set. I’d work any gig just to get face time with a Director. I’d grab their contact info and bug them for a chance to shadow! So, be persistent.

I’ve got a massive community for filmmakers comment 'JOIN' to be part of it. Meet other filmmakers from anywhere in the world👇

This video features one of the strangest survival strategies in the ocean: garden eels can spend their lives anchored inside sandy burrows, with only their bodies extending into the water. Instead of roaming around like many other fish, they stay close to their burrows while feeding on tiny drifting organisms carried by ocean currents.

What makes their behavior even more fascinating is reproduction. Their colonies can look like an underwater field of plants gently swaying with the current, but those “plants” are actually living fish constantly watching their surroundings.

Their burrows provide protection and a secure place to retreat whenever danger approaches. It’s a remarkable example of how an animal can build its entire lifestyle around staying in one safe location.

It actually touches on a couple of very common misconceptions about both water and electricity.
To understand why fish aren’t constantly being electrocuted, we first need to look at how electricity behaves when it enters a body of water.
1. The Path of Least Resistance
Electrical current is “lazy”; it will almost entirely flow through the path of least electrical resistance.
While pure water is actually an excellent insulator, the water in lakes, rivers, and oceans is full of dissolved salts and minerals (ions) that make it a great conductor. A fish’s body—covered in scales, slime, and oils—typically has a higher electrical resistance than the surrounding water, especially in the ocean. Because the water is a better conductor than the fish, the electricity simply flows around the fish rather than going through it.
2. Surface Dissipation
When a massive electrical discharge, like a lightning strike, hits a body of water, the current doesn’t plunge straight down into the depths. Instead, it spreads out horizontally across the surface.
The electrical energy dissipates radially and weakens drastically the deeper it goes. Because most fish live and swim below the surface layer of the water, the intense electrical charge passes right over their heads, leaving them completely unharmed.
3. Rapid Dilution of Energy
Bodies of water are massive. While a lightning strike contains an extraordinary amount of voltage (often hundreds of millions of volts), that energy is rapidly diluted as it expands outward into a giant three-dimensional volume of water. Just a short distance away from the direct impact point, the electrical field is completely neutralized.
Are fish ever affected?
Yes, under the right (or wrong) circumstances, fish absolutely can be electrocuted:
Direct Hits: If a fish happens to be swimming right at the surface exactly where a lightning bolt strikes, the sheer localized energy will likely kill it.

🌌 The Double-Slit Experiment Changed Our Understanding of Reality 🤯

One of the most famous experiments in quantum physics reveals just how different the microscopic world can be from our everyday experience.

When individual photons are sent toward two narrow slits and no which-path information is obtained, the results build up into an interference pattern—a pattern characteristic of wave-like quantum behavior. Even when photons are sent one at a time, the overall pattern gradually emerges. 🌊✨

But when an experimental setup allows scientists to determine which slit the photon passed through, the interference pattern disappears. The results instead become consistent with the two possible paths being distinguishable.

The important part is that the photon isn't somehow "aware" that it's being watched. 👁️❌

In quantum mechanics, obtaining which-path information requires a physical interaction with the system. That interaction changes the quantum state and can destroy the coherence needed for interference.

This is one of the reasons the experiment is so profound. It shows that at the quantum level, measurement isn't simply passive observation—it is a physical process that can affect what outcomes are possible.

The double-slit experiment doesn't prove that human consciousness creates reality. Instead, it demonstrates something even more fascinating: quantum systems don't always behave like ordinary classical objects with definite paths that we can simply observe without consequence. ⚛️

More than a century after its early forms were demonstrated, the double-slit experiment remains one of the clearest windows into the strange rules governing the quantum world.

The deeper we explore quantum mechanics, the more our everyday intuition begins to break down. 🌌🔬

Why is Mercury prohibited on airplanes? ✈️⚠️

Mercury is one of the few metals that remains liquid at room temperature. If it spills inside an aircraft, it doesn't just roll around—it can seep into tiny cracks and joints.

For centuries, Galileo Galilei challenged one of the biggest misconceptions in science by proposing that, in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of their mass. It sounded impossible in an era when a feather clearly drifted to the ground while a heavy stone crashed down in seconds. But Galileo understood that what we observe every day is influenced by Earth's atmosphere, not by gravity itself. In a vacuum, where air is completely removed, a feather and a bowling ball accelerate downward together at approximately 9.8 metres per second squared, reaching the ground at the exact same moment. It was a simple idea that completely changed our understanding of motion and laid the foundation for modern physics.

The reason is beautifully balanced: gravity pulls more strongly on heavier objects because they have more mass, but those same objects also possess greater inertia, making them equally harder to accelerate. These two effects cancel each other out perfectly, giving every object the same acceleration in free fall. The famous vacuum experiments carried out centuries later confirmed Galileo's prediction beyond doubt, turning what was once a controversial theory into one of the greatest demonstrations in scientific history. It's a powerful reminder that sometimes the truth isn't always what our eyes first lead us to believe.

When a bottle filled with water has holes in its side and is held stationary, water sprays out because of the hydrostatic pressure inside the liquid. At a depth h below the free surface, the pressure is p = p₀ + ρgh which is greater than atmospheric pressure p₀ by an amount ρgh, where ρ is the density of water and g is gravitational acceleration. This pressure difference produces a net outward force that accelerates the water through the holes.
The situation changes completely when the bottle is allowed to fall freely. In the freely falling frame of the bottle, both the bottle and the water accelerate downward with the same acceleration g. As a result, the effective gravitational field inside the bottle becomes approximately zero, so the hydrostatic pressure gradient disappears. Since the pressure at all points in the liquid becomes nearly uniform and equal to atmospheric pressure, there is no longer a pressure difference available to drive the water out through the holes. Physically, the water is in a transient state of weightlessness, analogous to astronauts orbiting Earth, where fluids no longer “settle” under gravity. Hence, during free fall, the water ceases to spray from the holes.

When hundreds of pounds of ice meet molten lava, the temperature difference is extreme. Lava often reaches roughly 700°C to 1,200°C, while ice sits at around 0°C.

The moment the ice contacts the lava, heat begins flowing rapidly from the lava into the ice. The ice melts, but the most dramatic effect comes from the water produced during melting.

As the surface of the ice heats, liquid water can rapidly transition into steam. Under the right conditions, a layer of vapor forms between the water and the intensely hot lava. This vapor layer acts as temporary insulation, slowing direct heat transfer. This phenomenon is known as the Leidenfrost effect.

If large amounts of ice and water interact with sufficiently hot lava, rapid steam production can also disturb and fragment the molten material. The expanding steam seeks to escape, potentially causing splashing or explosive interactions.

But 300 pounds of ice does not simply “extinguish” a large mass of lava. The outcome depends on the lava’s temperature, volume, composition, surface area and how the ice contacts the molten rock.

The underlying physics is a battle between thermal energy and phase changes. Lava loses heat while ice absorbs energy first to melt and then, if enough heat is available, to convert water into steam.

So the spectacular reaction is not magic. It is thermodynamics happening at an extreme temperature difference.

Osho passed away on January 19, 1990, in Pune. Despite controversy, his influence endures through books, discourses, and meditation centers worldwide.

Passive Gravitational Filtration: Notice the elevated slotted dome at the center of the basin. The slots act as a physical mesh filter. Continuous Overhead Rinsing: Watch how the basin fills with water without spilling out the sides, even with the tap running continuously. The internal drainage pathway is calibrated to balance the water inflow rate, creating a self-regulating, continuous cycle of clean water washing the fruit while dirty water is constantly expelled from the base.

After building Apple into one of the pioneers of the personal computer industry, Jobs was famously forced out of the company in 1985. During his absence, Apple struggled with declining sales, an unfocused product lineup, and mounting financial losses. By the time Jobs returned in 1997, the company was weeks away from running out of cash and had lost more than $1 billion the previous year.

Jobs believed Apple’s recovery depended on rebuilding the company’s foundation ,rather than focusing on cutting costs or engineering short-term profits. He simplified the product lineup, invested heavily in product design, strengthened Apple’s culture, and assembled a leadership team capable of executing a long-term vision. His belief was that if the company got its products, strategy, and people right, financial performance would naturally follow. Over the next decade, Apple introduced the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad, becoming one of the most valuable companies in history and today worth more than $4.9 trillion. Jobs’ statement proves that lasting businesses are built by getting the fundamentals right first, because strong financial results are usually the outcome of great execution, not the starting objective.

1. 💾 No one sentence concept
If you can't explain your game in one sentence, it's not clear enough yet

2. 💾 Starting with a huge idea
My first "game" was basically an MMO in my head haha (typical rookie mistake) start with something small you can always grow from there

3. 💾 Polishing before it's fun
Im still guilty of this one. I'll spend hours on the UI and animating stuff before I know if the core loop is even fun

4. 💾 Skipping version control
Lost two weeks of work to a corrupted file multiple times. Use Git from day one, don't be silly like me and save yourself from future stress 😂 (this might be the biggest one)

5. 💾 Ignoring performance too long
Waiting until the end to optimize means rebuilding half your systems, try to study how to optimize each part of the game as youre making it

6. 💾 Skipping localization early
Adding languages later means rewriting UI, strings, and basically redoing tons of stuff. Doesn't mean you need to translate the game imidietlly but you can atleast set it up for future if needed

7. 💾 Afraid to cut features
I held onto ideas that clearly weren't working out just because i didn't want to feel like I "wasted time"

8. 💾 Building my own engine
I built my own tools instead of shipping a game, there are many tools out there already to save your time

9. 💾 Working in isolation
Building in silence killed my motivation more than once. Share progress early, feedback, no matter if it's positive or negative, helps keep you going the right way

10. 💾 Adding not necessary features
I kept making things nobody requested instead of testing what I already had (scope creep alert)

I'm currently making a new game and hope you might follow this journey for more tips! ☕️🙌

Day 59: Optimization
If there was a final boss for game development, I’d argue it’s optimization. In order to get the level size maps to an acceptable range, I had to refactor the legacy inventory database by migrating from a monolithic Data Table to decentralized Primary Data Assets with asynchronous loading. By loading 3D meshes, materials, and UI icons dynamically on demand rather than on level startup, I reduced the prototype level’s memory footprint by over eighty percent. Memory usage dropped from 3.0 gigabytes to just 498 Megabytes, and we saved 800 Megabytes of disk space. So now there’s faster load times and smoother gameplay.

Video games are all smoke and mirrors, and our puzzle game Floor Plan: Slap Out Of It! is no exception. Even though all the floors are supposed to exist in one tower together, it was causing performance issues to have them all stacked on top of one another like they would be in real life. So we had to position them in really odd places throughout the game world.

Because of their positioning, it didn’t really make sense to smoothly move the elevator between them for a number of reasons. Not the least of which was the elevator clipping into other floors along the way. So instead, the elevator teleports to each floor and then we fake the movement so it feels right from the player’s perspective.

Sederhana, indah, tapi punya manfaat.

Survival Architecture Indonesia bukan tentang bertahan hidup karena kekurangan.

Survival Architecture Indonesia adalah cara berpikir untuk memanfaatkan setiap ruang, setiap waktu, dan setiap potensi agar kehidupan menjadi lebih mandiri.

Pagi ini, hanya beberapa menit sebelum berangkat, saya membantu istri saya menanam microgreen, salah satu superfood yang dapat dipanen dalam hitungan hari.

Inilah yang saya sebut Survival Architecture Indonesia.

Bukan menunggu lahan luas.
Bukan menunggu pensiun.
Bukan menunggu keadaan ideal.

Tetapi memulai dari apa yang kita miliki hari ini.

Dari lorong sempit harus lahir solusi besar.

Setiap jengkal ruang memiliki potensi.
Setiap pagi adalah kesempatan.
Setiap warga dapat menjadi teladan.

Karena perubahan tidak dimulai dari pidato, tetapi dari kebiasaan kecil yang dilakukan setiap hari.

Jangan terwarnai oleh keadaan. Kitalah yang harus mewarnai keadaan.

Mari manfaatkan ruang, waktu, dan pengetahuan untuk membangun keluarga yang lebih sehat, lingkungan yang lebih mandiri, dan Indonesia yang lebih tangguh.

Itulah Survival Architecture Indonesia.

Snapdragons should be planted at two times: Fall or Late Winter/very early spring. The key for either planting time if you want long, strong stems is to make sure you’re planting them out so that they’ll get cold growing weeks AND that you pick the right grouping for your climate. I personally prefer fall as it’s easy to ensure they get enough cold.

For fall planting, if you’re in zones 7 and up, it’s definitely time to start getting your snapdragon seeds so you have time for the little plants to get established before frost. Honestly, I’d even try this in zone 6b, because snaps are excessively cold hardy. Otherwise, save this to start them early next year!

I’m posting this a little early, so ya’ll have time to see it in time. Your goal should be to have 1 inch plants transplanted out 4 weeks before your first frost date. This allows them to establish their root systems before the cold hits, which is important for winter survival. So for me in zone 8b, that means that I want snapdragon seedlings planted out by end of September/early October.

Why is cold so important? Low temperatures slow down the growth of the plant, which causes hardy annuals to focus more on a very strong and robust root system. All of this stored energy turns into longer, more robust stems and flowers once temperatures get warm enough for them to grow again! Also, snapdragons REALLY are hardy. Mine easily handle 16 degrees F without any extra protection.

1. Make sure you’re growing the right grouping for your climate and when you’re growing them. Different varieties are bred for different times of year. What group a variety is in, should always be listed when you’re buying seed.

India’s Got Latent is an Indian comedy-based talent show created and hosted by Samay Raina. Unlike traditional talent competitions, the show’s twist is that contestants predict their own score before performing.

Here’s how it works:
• Contestants perform any talent—comedy, singing, dancing, magic, unusual skills, or anything entertaining.
• Before performing, they predict the score they think they’ll receive (typically on a 10-point scale).
• A panel of judges scores the performance.
• If the contestant’s average score matches their prediction exactly, they win the prize.

The show became popular because of:
• Its unscripted and humorous interactions.
• Roasting and banter between the host, judges, and contestants.
• Frequent appearances by well-known comedians, creators, and celebrities as guest judges.
• Viral clips shared across social media.

The show also faced controversy in early 2025 after remarks made on an episode featuring several internet personalities drew criticism, leading to public backlash, legal complaints, and the temporary removal of episodes from YouTube. Following this, the creators announced changes before continuing the series.

Overall, India’s Got Latent is best known for blending a talent competition with improv comedy and audience interaction, making it very different from conventional reality talent shows.

Scarlett Johansson shares why she speaks up when an instinct hits her on set. If she feels there’s something else she wants to try, she’ll ask for another take, because she’d rather ask than leave set wishing she had trusted that impulse. 👀🎥

But every director works differently. Some encourage exploration and improv, while others want you to follow the script and their direction exactly. A professional actor needs to be ready for both. 🎯

👇🏼 Tips for actors on set:

• 💡 Trust your instincts: If a new choice feels truthful, don’t automatically ignore it.
• 🎬 Read your director: Learn how much freedom they want you to bring to the scene.
• 🙋‍♀️ Don’t be afraid to ask questions: If you have more to give, respectfully asking for another take never hurts.

🎭Bonus acting tip —

Never try to create a character that is completely different from yourself for an audition.

Giving the character a completely different voice, accent, and body language without truly internalizing those external elements carries a high risk of turning the performance into a CARICATURE.

Because if you haven’t internalized these external elements enough, they can start looking like something you’re doing rather than something the character is naturally doing.

Don’t try to become someone else. Find the character within yourself.

Ahmed Al-Waeli (1928–2003) was an Iraqi Islamic scholar, renowned Shi’a preacher, poet, and writer. He was born in the holy city of Najaf, Iraq, on September 3, 1928, into a distinguished religious and literary family. His father, Sheikh Hassoun Al-Waeli, was a respected religious scholar, poet, and orator who had a profound influence on his education and character. Ahmed Al-Waeli memorized the Holy Qur’an at an early age and pursued his religious studies at the Hawza of Najaf.

Alongside his religious education, he completed his academic studies, earning a bachelor’s degree in Arabic Language and Islamic Studies from the College of Fiqh in Najaf, followed by a master’s degree from the University of Baghdad and a Ph.D. in Islamic Studies from Cairo University.

Al-Waeli began delivering religious sermons at a young age and became one of the most influential Husayni orators in the Islamic world. He was admired for his eloquence and his unique ability to combine Islamic teachings with Arabic literature, history, philosophy, and rational analysis. His sermons promoted moderation, dialogue, moral values, and respect for differing opinions.

In addition to his work as a preacher, he was an accomplished poet and prolific author who produced numerous books and lectures on Islamic thought, Arabic literature, history, and contemporary social issues.

In 1979, Al-Waeli left Iraq because of the political circumstances at the time and continued his scholarly and preaching activities while living abroad for many years. Following the political changes in Iraq in 2003, he returned to his homeland.

Ahmed Al-Waeli passed away in Baghdad on July 14, 2003. According to his will, he was buried in Najaf near the shrine of Kumayl ibn Ziyad. He left behind a rich intellectual and religious legacy that continues to inspire millions of people across the Islamic world. He is widely remembered as “The Dean of the Husayni Pulpit.”

In the finished film, directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller preserve that same emotional truth while removing much of the explanation. Instead, Ryan Gosling’s performance, the pacing, the music, and the silence reveal everything Grace has been holding inside.

The scene offers a more human take on the traditional heroic sacrifice. Grace still risks his life to save Earth, but that does not mean he wants to die. His fear does not make him less courageous. It makes his courage feel real.

The earlier draft explains the revelation beautifully. The film finds a quieter, more cinematic way to let us feel it.

Sometimes the most powerful adaptation choices come from knowing what can remain unsaid.

David Bowie’s Philosophy on Art and Creativity

In the 1997 documentary Inspirations, David Bowie shared his thoughts on why people create art and what drives true creativity.

For Bowie, art was a way of exploring identity—a process of understanding who you are and where you fit within the wider world. He believed that creativity loses its power when artists become focused on meeting expectations or pleasing an audience. The most meaningful work, in his view, comes from taking risks, exploring uncertainty, and entering unfamiliar territory.

Although psychedelics have often been associated with artistic inspiration, Bowie had a different perspective. He experimented with LSD a few times but felt that his own imagination was already powerful enough without external influences. In a 1976 interview with Playboy, he explained that the experience produced interesting visuals but did not provide anything he felt he couldn’t already access through his own creativity.

Bowie’s approach reflected a belief shared by many great artists: the most important discoveries often come from looking inward and having the courage to explore ideas without knowing exactly where they will lead.

These were big pills to swallow...

1. Stop waiting for the "perfect" project. You have to give yourself permission to make something "bad." You have to make mistakes to figure out what actually looks good. If you spend all your time planning the perfect movie that will never have any problems, you’ll never actually hit the record button. Just go make something messy…you’ll get better every time.

2. In short films, action is king. Show us what’s happening rather than explaining it. In a short film, you don't have two hours to explain a character’s whole life story. Instead of having people sit around and talk about their feelings, show us the story through the camera and the action. Keep it moving! Shorts are best when focused on an event. Your audience will be way more into it, and it makes editing a lot easier.

3. Act like a pro (even if your "crew" is just your friends). Treat your "set" with respect, even if it’s just your backyard and your brother is holding the flashlight! He holds a PhD, degrees in history, law and sociology, and once sat in one of the most powerful bureaucratic seats in the country. He quietly walked away from all of it to teach in a rented room in Mukherjee Nagar because he believed something more important was being ignored.

Dr. Vikas Divyakirti was born in 1973 in Bhiwani, Haryana, to two parents who worked as educators with a deep, almost inherited devotion to the Hindi language. That environment shaped the entire direction of his life. He collected an extraordinary breadth of academic credentials at Delhi University, history, Hindi literature, sociology, law and eventually a doctorate, an academic depth rarely seen in someone who would go on to run a coaching institute.

In 1996, he cleared the UPSC Civil Services Examination on his very first attempt, a feat that eludes most aspirants across multiple tries, and was posted to the Ministry of Home Affairs. He had reached the position that defines success for an entire generation of Indian students competing in one of the toughest examinations on earth.

He resigned within a year.

What pulled him away was not dissatisfaction with the role itself, but a growing awareness of an inequality he could not ignore. India's UPSC coaching ecosystem was overwhelmingly built for English-medium, urban, financially comfortable students. Hindi-medium aspirants, often from small towns and modest backgrounds with genuinely serious talent, were treated as an afterthought, given weaker materials and less mentorship despite facing the exact same exam.

In 1999 he founded Drishti IAS specifically to correct that imbalance. He taught dense conceptual material in accessible, rigorous Hindi, refusing to dilute the substance simply because the language changed.

Today Drishti IAS reaches crores of students through YouTube alone, students who could never have afforded Delhi's coaching corridors, proving that serious preparation and financial exclusivity were never actually required to go together.

He left a government chair that thousands dream of reaching. He built a classroom that reaches millions instead.

The brain naturally overestimates how much other people notice and remember your actions. This makes ordinary situations feel like public performances.

Let’s drop a bunch of people on a dirty street. Zero fine.
Each wrapper on the ground is permission for the next. Almost everyone drops theirs.
Sweep them back. Their trash is gone — just the original few left. And now, a ten dollar fine.
Only one in five drops now. Bin sight opens up, and it falls to five percent.
Clean sweep. Even those last wrappers are gone. Bare floor — and everybody walks theirs to a bin.
Fine drops back to zero. Still nobody litters. People copy what’s around them more than they read the rule.

Broken Windows Theory says disorder is contagious. A visible piece of litter is not just trash — it is a social signal. It tells the next person that dropping is normal here, that nobody is watching, and that the cost of being the one who makes it worse is already gone. Formal rules still exist on paper, but the environment writes the rule people actually follow. Raise the expected cost of getting caught — a fine, a camera, a bin you cannot miss — and the same crowd throws less, because the risk is now readable. Take the signal away entirely and the threshold flips: on a clean floor, the first wrapper is the expensive one. Nobody wants to be the person who breaks the norm. That is why a fine can drop back to zero and littering still stays near zero. Deterrence changes the calculation. Cleanliness changes the default. People copy what’s around them more than they read the rule.

Is metacognition a superpower or a curse?

Recently when I shared that metacognition is one of the highest forms of intelligence, many people disagreed.

“It’s a curse.” “My brain never stops thinking.” And honestly, I understand why.

Metacognition is the ability to think about your own thinking. In psychology, it’s a key part of self-awareness because it allows you to notice your thoughts, question your beliefs, and reflect on your decisions instead of running on autopilot (Fleming, S. M., & Dolan, R. J. (2012)).

But here’s where things get complicated.

When your nervous system feels safe and regulated, metacognition strengthens emotional intelligence, critical thinking, resilience, and better decision-making.

When your nervous system is stuck in survival mode, that same ability can turn into rumination, overthinking, anxiety, self-doubt, and mental exhaustion.

The ability itself isn’t the problem. It’s whether your mind is observing your thoughts... or getting trapped inside them.

Your thoughts are data, not commands. Metacognition gives you the power to question them instead of automatically believing them.

The goal isn’t to think less.

It’s to build a mind that knows which thoughts deserve your attention, and which ones deserve to be let go.

Has metacognition felt more like a superpower or a curse in your life?

Tap the patellar tendon, and a remarkable neural circuit fires almost instantly.

For years, salt has been blamed for increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

However, long term research published in The Lancet challenged that assumption. Researchers found that people consuming moderate amounts of sodium had a lower cardiovascular risk than those following extremely low sodium diets.

History offers another perspective. Ancient cultures regularly consumed natural, mineral rich salt without viewing it as the health threat many people associate it with today.

Neuroscience helps explain why sodium matters. It is essential for hydration, nerve signaling, muscle contraction, brain function, and the electrical activity that allows your neurons to communicate. Every thought, memory, and movement depends on sodium and potassium working together.

Reducing sodium too aggressively can activate hormones such as renin and aldosterone, which may increase physiological stress and cardiovascular strain in some people.

The relationship between salt and health is more complex than many headlines suggest. Factors such as overall diet, potassium intake, kidney function, and individual health all influence how sodium affects the body.

**Polymorphism** in mineralogy is when the exact same chemical compound can crystallize into two or more completely different structures, same atoms, same formula, but arranged in different patterns.

That difference in atomic arrangement changes everything: the shape, the density, the hardness, even how the mineral behaves.

A perfect example of this is **calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)**.

In nature, it takes on two very different forms: **calcite** and **aragonite**.

Calcite crystallizes in a trigonal (rhombohedral) system, forms under lower pressure and more stable conditions, and is the more common, more stable form over geological time.

Aragonite, on the other hand, crystallizes in an orthorhombic system, often forms under higher pressure or in biological settings (like inside mollusk shells and coral skeletons), and is actually metastable, meaning over long periods, it can slowly transform back into calcite.

Other well-known examples of polymorphism include :

Diamond and graphite (both pure carbon), pyrite and marcasite (both FeS₂), quartz, tridymite, and cristobalite (all SiO₂), and kyanite, andalusite, and sillimanite (all Al₂SiO₅).

Have you ever seen hikers rubbing wet sponges or rollers onto dry stepping stones and wondered what they were doing? While it might look like they are just making the path slippery, it is actually a clever safety tactic to protect everyone on the trail!
By applying water to the surface of a rock, hikers can quickly determine its density and structural integrity. If the water disappears into the stone almost instantly, it means the rock is full of tiny gaps. This porosity allows water to seep deep inside, where it can freeze, expand, and crack the rock apart from within—making it incredibly brittle, unstable, and dangerous to step on.
On the other hand, if the water sits on the surface and takes forever to soak in, the rock is dense and solid. This is exactly what you want for a stepping stone that people are trusting with their full weight. When a rock fails this test, hikers will often kick it over and replace it with a much safer, sturdier alternative to keep the trail secure for the next person.

A large open pit blast releases an enormous amount of stored chemical energy, and it is over in less than a second. What looks like one event is actually hundreds of separate detonations, sequenced to the millisecond.

Rock breaks in two stages.

- Detonation front: the explosive column reacts at 3,000 to 6,000 m/s, generating borehole pressures in the gigapascal range. The shock wave crushes rock immediately around the hole, then radiates outward. Rock is roughly ten times weaker in tension than compression, so much of the fracturing happens when that wave reflects off a free face and returns as a tensile pulse.
- Gas expansion: microseconds later, the detonation products expand into the new cracks, wedge them open, and heave the broken mass forward into a muckpile.

Design controls everything.

- Burden is the distance from the hole to the nearest free face. Too large and the charge is confined, producing oversize rock and heavy ground vibration. Too small and gas vents early, throwing flyrock.
- Stemming, usually angular crushed aggregate rather than loose drill cuttings, plugs the collar and holds gas pressure in long enough to do useful work.
- Delays of roughly 5 to 25 milliseconds between holes let each charge fire into ground that has already started moving, creating a fresh free face for the next one.

Most bulk explosive is now ANFO or emulsion, pumped or augered into the hole on site. The ingredients are inert until mixed, which is why a blast crew can drive fertiliser and fuel oil to a pit and only make an explosive at the collar.

Fragmentation is the real product. Finer, more uniform rock moves faster through the crusher and draws less mill power, so extra spend on explosive often pays for itself downstream.

The explosive does not move the mountain. The timing does.

Mohammed Abdullah Qahtani est un conférencier, auteur et ingénieur en sécurité informatique saoudien devenu un symbole mondial de résilience après avoir remporté en 2015 le Championnat du monde de prise de parole en public de Toastmasters, la compétition de discours la plus prestigieuse au monde.

Du bégaiement à l’ovation debout.

Qahtani a grandi avec un bégaiement sévère. Il avait du mal à parler couramment, a subi du harcèlement et n’a prononcé son premier mot qu’à l’âge de six ans.
La communication n’était pas sa force ; c’était son plus grand obstacle.

En 2009, il a rejoint un club Toastmasters avec un seul objectif : corriger sa faiblesse.

Ce qui a suivi fut le résultat d’une pratique acharnée, d’une discipline constante et d’un positionnement intelligent, utilisant l’humour et le storytelling comme des atouts plutôt que de cacher ses défauts.

Il n’a pas éliminé sa faiblesse.
Il a appris à la dépasser.
En 2015, après six mois de compétition et sept tours éliminatoires — face à plus de 33 000 participants — il a remporté le championnat du monde à Las Vegas.
Premier Arabe à gagner ce titre.

Premier et seul Saoudien à l’avoir accompli.
Son discours intitulé « The Power of Words » (Le pouvoir des mots) est devenu une véritable leçon magistrale de narration émotionnelle et d’impact.

Leçon : votre plus grande faiblesse peut devenir votre marque personnelle la plus forte, si vous apprenez à l’utiliser à votre avantage.

I only did this because I was having a more challenging day with my speech, and I knew I was going to Toastmasters, a public speaking club, later that day.

I’m trying to overcome my stutter by throwing myself into difficult situations - environments I’d usually avoid like the plague.

I was very aware of how difficult my speech felt that day. So instead of throwing myself straight into the deep end at Toastmasters and hoping I could swim, I decided to do something that was still very challenging, but just a little easier.

That way, I could build some confidence and get a small win before taking on the bigger challenge.

Introducing myself is already pretty hard because I often struggle on my name. A drive-thru is also a situation I don’t feel completely comfortable in, so I thought, why not combine the two and make it an even bigger challenge?

It wasn’t perfect at all.

But that wasn’t the goal.

The goal was to feel some discomfort now, so that later, standing in a room full of people and delivering a speech wouldn’t feel like such a huge leap.

1. Kenali Audiensmu!
Sebelum public speaking, kamu perlu tahu siapa audiensmu. Kamu bisa tanyain ke panitianya, beberapa pertanyaan berikut:
▪️Apa latar belakang mereka?
▪️Apa minat mereka
▪️Apa yang mereka harapkan dari penampilanmu?
Setelah kamu mengetahui bbrp pertanyaan tsb, kamu sesuaikan bahasa dengan audiensmu! Bikin mereka merasa lagi ngobrol langsung sm kamu ya!

2. Story telling
Bagikan pengalaman pribadi kamu yang relevan dengan topik yang dibahas saat itu,
dengan kamu membagikan cerita ini membuat audiens lebih relate dan mudah diingat.

3. Kasih Pertanyaan
Kasih pertanyaan ke audiens bisa membuat audiens berpartisipasi. Hal ini dapat membuat mereka merasa terlibat dan penting. Tapi, kamu perlu kasih jeda waktu supaya audiens bisa menjawab pertanyaanmu ya!

Never introduce yourself in an interview like this, my friend.

The interview starts with the most underrated question: tell me about yourself. And most people answer it the exact same way.

“My name is this. I studied at this college. I am from this city. I have this many years of experience. Thank you.”

That is not an introduction. That is a CV being read out loud.

✦

The interviewer already has your CV. He does not need you to narrate it back to him.

This question is not a formality. It is the first test — and most people fail it before the interview has even started.

Here is what a great answer actually does.

It tells a story. Not your life story — one specific story that explains who you are, what you are good at, and why you are sitting in that chair. It connects your past to this exact role in a way that makes the interviewer think: “This man knows exactly why he is here.”

✦

Something like this:

“I have spent the last three years building sales teams from scratch in early-stage startups. I have made every mistake possible, learnt what actually moves the numbers, and I am now at a point where I want to bring that experience to a company that is ready to scale. That is why I applied here.”

Sixty seconds. No hometown. No college name, unless it is relevant.

Just clarity, confidence, and a reason you belong in that room.

✦

The first thirty seconds of an interview set the tone for everything that follows, my friend.

Own them.

After 20+ years in recruiting, I’ve interviewed thousands of candidates.

And here’s something most people don’t realize:

The interview starts before the “real” questions do.

You walk in.

They offer you water.

You’re shown where to sit.

There’s an awkward pause.

Someone makes small talk.

Those moments may feel meaningless…

But they can reveal a lot about how comfortable you are under mild pressure.

Not because accepting water is some secret hiring test.

It isn’t.

What matters is HOW you handle the moment.

Do you instantly say yes because you think that’s what they want?

Do you over-explain why you don’t want it?

Do you look uncomfortable making a simple decision?

Or do you just decide?

“Water would be great, thank you.”

Or:

“No thanks, I’m good.”

Then move on.

That sounds ridiculously simple.

But confidence often looks simple.

Strong candidates don’t spend the entire interview trying to perform the “correct” behavior.

They listen.

They think.

They answer.

They’re comfortable with a little silence.

And they don’t apologize for every decision they make.

That same behavior shows up later when I ask:

“What salary are you looking for?”

“Why are you leaving?”

“Are you interviewing elsewhere?”

“Do you have any questions for me?”

The lesson has nothing to do with water.

It’s this:

Stop trying to guess what the interviewer wants you to say.

Listen to the question.

Think.

Then answer like someone who knows what they want.

That kind of composure gets noticed.

Don’t panic. Own it.

Never trash your old company. Redirect to growth.
“I’ve genuinely learned a lot there — but I’ve hit a ceiling. I’m looking for an environment where I can take on bigger challenges and align with my long-term goals.”

Never lowball yourself. Come prepared.
“Based on my research and the scope of this role, I’m looking at [X–Y range]. I’m open to discussing the full package.”

This isn’t small talk — it’s a culture fit test.
“Outside work, I [hobby] — which has actually helped me build [relevant skill]. It keeps me sharp and balanced.”

The answers aren’t just honest — they’re strategic. Every response should show self-awareness AND value.

O que faz uma cantora parecer elegante e feminina no palco? ✨🎤

Reagindo a essa interpretação de @voronina_valeria_ “All By Myself”, uma coisa me chamou muito a atenção: ela não entrega apenas técnica. Existe delicadeza, intenção e muita elegância na forma de cantar.

E isso não significa cantar fraco ou sem potência. Pelo contrário! Você pode ter uma voz enorme e, ainda assim, manter suavidade e refinamento.

✨ 5 detalhes que podem trazer mais elegância e feminilidade para a sua interpretação:

1. Não comece entregando toda a potência
Perceba o arzinho e a suavidade no início. Ela cria espaço para a música crescer. Elegância também está no contraste.

2. Faça movimentos mais conscientes
Não precisa movimentar o corpo o tempo inteiro. Gestos menores e intencionais podem transmitir muito mais segurança no palco.

3. Deixe os melismas mais definidos
Em vez de colocar muitas notas simplesmente para mostrar habilidade, escolha onde ornamentar. Ela faz melismas suaves, limpos e muito musicais.

4. Trabalhe as dinâmicas
Suave, médio, intenso… depois volte. Essa variação deixa a interpretação sofisticada e evita aquela sensação de cantar tudo com a mesma intensidade.

5. Não tente imitar a cantora original
Talvez essa seja a maior lição dessa apresentação. Você ouve All By Myself e lembra imediatamente de Celine Dion, mas ela não tenta ser Celine. Ela canta com o próprio timbre e preserva a própria identidade.

E para mim, isso é extremamente artístico.

Elegância vocal não é fazer mais. Muitas vezes, é saber exatamente onde fazer menos. ✨

Qual desses 5 detalhes você mais precisa desenvolver quando canta? 👇
